title: Lakshmi rises from the ocean
hookLine: the gods churn the ocean, the moon rises, then Lakshmi on a lotus: the goddess the Sri Sukta paints in gold and moonlight
carry: Lakshmi is Shakti as abundance, not only money
last: I BREATHE OUT LIKE THE WIND.

lines: THE MOON RISES. THEN SRI, ON A LOTUS.
cards: Picture an ocean churned like milk into butter. The gods pull one end of a great serpent, the asuras pull the other, and a mountain spins in the sea between them.
In the Vishnu Purana's telling, wonders rise from the foam, one after another. The moon rises. More wonders follow.

And then, standing on a lotus, shining, comes Sri, the goddess Lakshmi. Elephants pour water over her from golden jars, and she goes to Vishnu. Today, the hymn Hindus still chant when lamps are lit for her: the Sri Sukta.

teach.h: SUKTA: A HYMN. SRI: RADIANCE, FORTUNE.
teach.b: Sukta means hymn, and sri is heard as radiance, beauty and good fortune all at once.
The hymn's first verse paints her, in paraphrase: golden in color, wearing garlands of gold and silver, shining like the moon, made of gold. Notice the pair. Gold you can earn, store and spend.

teach.h: THE MOON AND LAKSHMI, FROM ONE SEA.
teach.b: And in the churning story, the moon and Lakshmi rise from the same sea. Some readers hear the hymn's point there: the fortune it asks for is bright like gold and freely given like moonlight. Here's the teaching.
Lakshmi is Shakti, the goddess's power, seen as abundance. Not only money: food on the table, health, a peaceful house, a good name. That's why Lakshmi Puja on Diwali night isn't a bank meeting.
Families clean the house, draw rangoli at the door, light lamps and leave the way open, because abundance is a goddess you welcome, not a thing you grab.

Business families set their new account books before her too: work honored, not money worshipped for its own sake. Teachers read the hymn more than one way. Some keep it plain, a household asking not to go without.
Others hear it inwardly, as a prayer for the brightness of a good life. The hymn doesn't choose. Today: we measure a good month in one number.
The Sri Sukta's portrait counts in gold and moonlight both.

how: The Sri Sukta is chanted in Lakshmi worship, including in some homes and temples at Diwali, with lamps lit and offerings set before an image of the goddess.

o: a Vedic hymn calling Sri, called Lakshmi, to come
a Sanskrit list of a temple's gold and silver
a song of thanks sung only after a harvest

games.q: the hymn's first look — tap the pairs.

s: in the Vishnu Purana, Lakshmi rises from the churned ocean
after the moon and other wonders, Sri rises on a lotus and goes to Vishnu.
the hymn's first picture of her is golden, garlanded and moonlit
golden in color, garlands of gold and silver, shining like the moon.
Lakshmi stands for money and nothing else
she is abundance: food, health, a peaceful house, a good name. sri means radiance and fortune at once.

games.q: a friend says Lakshmi Puja is just praying to get rich. by the Sri Sukta and the churning story, what's the fuller answer?
o: fair: it's a puja for cash.
Lakshmi is abundance: food, health, peace, a good name, welcomed home.
it's to keep the gods from envying your money.
games.why: Lakshmi is Shakti seen as abundance. the hymn paints her in gold and moonlight, and families welcome her with a clean house and lit lamps.

practice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that's like gold, something you worked for or keep safe, and hold it for a few breaths, with thanks.
Then bring to mind one thing like moonlight, something good you never earned and can't own: a friend's laugh, a clear night, a stranger's kindness.
If you pray, you can name them both before Lakshmi, or before God, in the words you already use.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. The hymn to Sri, called Lakshmi, which opens by seeing her golden, garlanded in gold and silver, and shining like the moon.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Sri Sukta, the hymn to Sri, the goddess also called Lakshmi.

carryVoice: Your line: Lakshmi is Shakti as abundance, not only money. Gold you can keep; moonlight you can only see. That's today, done.
